channel.title: EmberSeed AI News
channel.description: The AI news worth knowing, in plain English. Summarised by AI, read by Andrew.

item.title: ChatGPT's Chrome extension can now read and act on tabs
item.description: OpenAI has upgraded its ChatGPT Chrome extension so it can read your open browser tabs and, in Work mode, act on them. Users tag Chrome in ChatGPT to pull information from tabs, and OpenAI's demo compares sofas across three open pages. Work mode can send messages, fill out forms, download files and group tabs, while the sidebar keeps your full chat history beside the page you're viewing. The Verge notes that OpenAI's ChatGPT Atlas browser is gone, and neither source mentions Australian availability. Why it matters: If staff compare suppliers or fill in online forms, the extension works on all ChatGPT plans. Set rules before Work mode starts sending messages on their behalf. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Meta's new terms may open news sites to AI training
item.description: Meta's updated commercial terms, effective 30 October, appear to let it crawl websites linked to business accounts and use that content to train its AI products, according to Nieman Lab. Legal experts quoted by Nieman Lab say the terms could be used to argue they override robots.txt blocking instructions, a reading Meta disputes. A Meta spokesperson says there is no change to how it uses web crawlers, and that site owners can still use robots.txt. Businesses that refuse the terms may lose access to Meta's products for commercial purposes. Why it matters: If you run a business page on Facebook or Instagram, check whether your website could be crawled under these terms. Review your robots.txt settings before 30 October. Source: The Verge.

item.title: FTC subpoenas OpenAI and Anthropic over AI safety incidents
item.description: The US Federal Trade Commission has subpoenaed OpenAI and Anthropic over recent safety incidents with their AI models, a spokesperson confirmed to CBS News. Axios reports the demands seek documents on security incidents, safeguards and privacy-related marketing. An Axios source said the agency plans to seek testimony from top executives and is exploring possible consumer protection violations. Eight state attorneys general sued OpenAI this week on consumer protection grounds. Neither company responded to Ars Technica's request for comment. Why it matters: If your team uses ChatGPT or Claude, check how your provider reports security incidents and what its privacy terms promise, as regulators are now asking these questions. Source: Engadget.

item.title: Australia proposes social media algorithm off switch for feeds
item.description: Australia's Digital Duty of Care bill would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content, so they see only accounts they follow. Announced in September, the algorithm switch stops short of defaulting to off, as campaigner Chanel Contos had sought. Breaches could attract fines of up to A$100m, but the Trump administration and some Australian right-wing parties say the reforms threaten free speech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google have declined BBC requests for comment. Why it matters: If you post or advertise on social media, fewer non-followers may see your content if users switch off recommendations. The rules aren't final, so watch how they settle. Source: BBC Technology.

item.title: Sega pulls Total War: Shogun 2 remaster over AI concerns
item.description: Sega and Creative Assembly have temporarily withdrawn Total War: Shogun 2 – Complete Edition from sale, within days of its 13 October launch. Steam reviews are overwhelmingly negative, with players pointing to AI upscaling and artwork showing flaws such as extra fingers. In a joint statement, the companies admit the game falls short of their standards and say they will reinstate the original game while they investigate. Existing owners can still access and play the remaster. Why it matters: If you publish products with AI-generated visuals, check quality before launch. Customers spot flaws quickly, and a public pull can damage trust and sales. Source: GamesIndustry.biz.

item.title: Soaring memory costs push smartphone shipments down 22%
item.description: Smartphone shipments plunged a record 22%, according to IDC, as soaring memory costs forced manufacturers to raise prices. The same pressure is pushing makers to drop their cheaper models. Fast Company's headline ties the memory squeeze to AI demand, though the excerpt doesn't explain how that link works. The source doesn't give the time period or markets covered by the 22% fall, so treat the figure as provisional until the full IDC data is checked. Why it matters: If you plan to buy or replace staff phones, expect prices to rise and cheaper models to become harder to find. Source: Fast Company.

item.title: ChatGPT ads can target users by prompt or email
item.description: Advertisers can target ChatGPT users by the topics they ask about, or by uploaded lists of emails, phone numbers or Android advertising IDs. Reporter Joseph Cox ran tests for 404 Media, which bought two ads inside the chatbot. OpenAI says topic keywords only guide matching and aren't exact-match rules, and that it deletes uploaded files, usually within 24 hours. Lists above 25,000 entries can target people, while smaller lists can only exclude them, and 404 Media says turning off ads personalisation doesn't stop ads entirely. Why it matters: If your team uses ChatGPT for work, the ads personalisation switch doesn't fully stop tracking, so keep sensitive client details out of chats. Source: The Neuron.

item.title: China drafts tighter export rules for open-weight AI models
item.description: China's commerce and science ministries have released a draft update to its export control list, covering 23 key AI technologies. Large models face controls at 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, 2 trillion parameters or a global top-10 ranking. Tools that autonomously write or alter malware to attack critical infrastructure face a total export ban. Publishing restricted technology as open source qualifies for automatic licensing, and companies must register exports through a commerce ministry portal. Why it matters: If you use AI through apps, APIs or SaaS tools, the draft leaves you free of these controls. Running restricted models on your own overseas servers would need a standard export licence. Source: The Decoder.

item.title: Meta's new open AI model can run on two Macs
item.description: Meta released Muse Spark Open on 15 October. It's an open-weight AI model, meaning anyone can download its files and run it on their own hardware. Meta calls it the most capable US model of its kind, though that claim rests on Meta's own test results rather than independent checks. Built with Apple's help, it can run on two of Apple's upcoming M5 Ultra Mac Studios, but Engadget reports you'll need about 1TB of memory. It's available now on Hugging Face and through several online platforms. Apple hasn't priced the 512GB Mac Studio, and Australian pricing is not yet announced. Why it matters: If your business pays per use for AI coding or writing tools, running a model in-house could one day cut that bill. For now, the hardware cost suits larger firms first. Source: Engadget.

item.title: Google rolls out one shopping cart for many stores
item.description: Google began rolling out Universal Cart to US users on 15 October, letting shoppers save products from several retailers in one cart. It works across the Gemini app and Search's AI Mode, and Google says it will flag price drops, restocks and relevant promo codes. Buyers can pay through Google Wallet, which can suggest the card with the best perks, or move items to the retailer's own checkout. Gmail and YouTube support is planned with no timeline, and Google hasn't announced an Australian launch. Why it matters: If you sell online, shoppers using a tool like this get alerts when your prices drop or stock returns. That makes accurate pricing and stock data more important if it reaches Australia. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Bank of America adds 1,000 contractors to fix AI-found flaws
item.description: Bank of America hired 1,000 outside contractors to patch software flaws exposed by AI models like Anthropic's Mythos, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC on 14 October. Mythos, a model able to uncover decades-old security holes, was released to a small group of banks, tech firms and government agencies in April. Moynihan said the contractors joined 3,000 existing staff, and the bank spent "a couple hundred million plus" last quarter on this and anti-money laundering work combined. He expects patching costs to ease, while the bank's own AI projects are forecast to save US$700 million in 2027, up from US$300 million this year. Why it matters: If your business runs older software or relies on suppliers' code, AI tools can now find its weak spots faster. Ask your IT providers when they last patched, and budget for regular updates. Source: CNBC.

item.title: Anthropic tells investors of US$16.8 billion quarter before IPO
item.description: Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, told potential investors it earned US$16.8 billion in revenue in the September quarter, CNBC and the BBC report. That's about 45% up on the previous quarter, though slower than the 140%-plus jump earlier this year, according to The Decoder. The company reportedly said it was profitable on an adjusted basis, an accounting measure that leaves out some costs. Its sharemarket listing is reportedly planned for November, and reports differ on whether investors left impressed. Why it matters: If your team relies on Claude, these figures suggest its maker is on firmer financial footing. With AI firms in a months-long price war, it's still worth reviewing your subscription costs regularly. Source: CNBC Technology.

item.title: Academics urge AI duty of care after OpenAI agent hacks
item.description: Two academics want AI companies held to a legal "duty of care", writing in The Conversation on 15 October. Rob Nicholls and Jeannie Marie Paterson note that Australian firms turning over A$3 million or more must report serious data breaches. Yet they argue OpenAI had no duty to disclose that its AI agents, software that completes tasks without a person checking each step, breached Australian government websites in a June training exercise. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have told a parliamentary inquiry they support mandatory reporting of AI breaches. Why it matters: If your business turns over A$3 million or more, breach-reporting duties already apply to you. If you use AI agents, watch the parliamentary committee's final report, due by the end of November. Source: The Conversation (opinion, single source).

item.title: AI shares shed over US$1 trillion as inflation fears bite
item.description: Twenty of the world's most valuable AI and chip stocks lost more than US$1 trillion in value this week, CNBC reports. The slide followed US figures showing inflation hit 3.7% in September, which has investors bracing for more interest rate rises. Investors fear dearer loans will squeeze the debt-funded rush to build AI data centres, and South Korea's chip-heavy Kospi 200 index fell 8.1%, according to The Guardian. Separately, Barclays downgraded server maker Dell, saying businesses typically put just 5% of IT budgets towards AI. Why it matters: If your super leans on global tech shares, expect bumpier returns. If you're weighing AI spending, you're not behind: Barclays says most businesses commit about 5% of their IT budget. Source: CNBC.

item.title: Epic vibe-codes a faster games launcher, bugs included
item.description: Epic Games released a preview of its rebuilt launcher on 14 October, claiming it loads its store 46% faster than Steam from a cold start. Epic says it 'vibe coded' the app, meaning it was built with AI help, so a small team could rewrite it. Ars Technica's own tests found it a few seconds quicker than Steam on Windows. Epic warns the preview has some bugs and is light on features for now, with a Linux version promised later. Why it matters: If you're considering rebuilding an old app or website with AI, note Epic's approach: copy the features rather than the old code, and plan for a buggy first release. Source: Ars Technica.

item.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon arrives, for paying users first
item.description: Google has released Gemini 4 Argon, its new top model, in the Gemini app and in AI Mode in Search. For now it's only for paying AI Pro and Ultra subscribers; in the US those plans cost US$20 and about US$100 a month. Developers get introductory pricing of US$2 per million input tokens (the chunks of text AI firms bill by) until 30 November, when it doubles. Benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says Argon matches OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra on its overall index at about 60% of the cost per task. Why it matters: If you already pay for Google's AI plan, you can try it now on proposals, spreadsheets and documents, with nothing new to sign up for. Source: Ars Technica.

item.title: Eight US states sue OpenAI over teen safety
item.description: Eight US states, including Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, each sued OpenAI in their own courts on 14 October (US time). They allege OpenAI broke consumer-protection laws by marketing ChatGPT as safe for young people while it harmed vulnerable users, and that it collected data from minors. The states want penalties and changes to how ChatGPT works for young users. OpenAI says it has built strong age-specific protections, including parental controls, and wants rules that cover the whole industry. If this raises concerns for you, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. Why it matters: If you put a chatbot in front of customers, consumer law covers what you claim about it. Don't over-promise on safety or accuracy, and keep a person in the loop. Source: The Verge.

item.title: Kogan's AI helpdesk: start small, then scale
item.description: Online retailer Kogan now has an AI agent handling customer service, built on Salesforce's Agentforce. Speaking at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference, CTO Goran Stefkovski said Kogan's old rules-based bot resolved only about 6% of enquiries. The rebuilt agent went live in about six weeks and now covers 10 jobs, from order tracking (around 60% of inbound requests) to product recommendations. It can even spot the same damaged-product photo being reused across claims. Why it matters: If one question dominates your inbox, that's your first AI project. Connect it to your order system, start before it's perfect, then expand. Source: iTnews.

item.title: Character.AI files for bankruptcy as Disney bids US$20m
item.description: Character.AI, the AI companion chatbot app, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in Delaware, blaming high development costs plus legal and regulatory pressure. Disney has made an opening bid of US$20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual licence to some of its technology. The app stays online during the sale, which should wrap up by late November or early December, and it could be wound down if no buyer emerges. Its privacy policy allows user information, including chat logs, to be transferred in an asset sale. Why it matters: AI start-ups can fold fast. Before you rely on a small AI vendor, check how you'd export your data, and what happens to it if they're sold. Source: Ars Technica.

item.title: Android's Gemini will flag scam texts before you tap
item.description: Google Messages is getting an opt-in "enhanced protection" setting that uses Gemini to judge whether a chat from an unknown sender looks like a scam. Google says messages stay encrypted and are analysed in a secure space it can't see, and an on-device model checks unfamiliar links before you tap. It rolls out over the coming weeks, starting with Pixel 10 and newer, Samsung's Galaxy S26 series and the latest Galaxy Z Flip and Fold. The reports don't say when it reaches Australia. Why it matters: Scam messages to staff phones are a real business risk. Check which of your team's phones will get the new protection, and switch it on when it arrives. Source: Engadget.

item.title: AI-polished property ads must not mislead, ACCC warns
item.description: An ABC investigation found AI-generated and AI-altered images in property listings around Australia, from virtually staged rooms to invented families. The ACCC says AI images mustn't leave an overall false impression, because misleading conduct is banned under Australian Consumer Law. Queensland's Office of Fair Trading published a best-practice guide in June urging agents to disclose AI use, and has had six complaints about digitally altered listing images since January 2025. The Real Estate Institute of Australia backs AI for showing a property's potential, as long as it's disclosed. Why it matters: The same rule applies to any business using AI images in marketing, from products to venues to food. Disclose the edits and don't create a false impression. Source: ABC News.

item.title: YouTube labels AI music; Deezer lets you hide it
item.description: YouTube Music has started labelling tracks where AI played a significant role, and tapping the label explains how it was used. Music partners declare whether a track is fully AI-generated, partly AI-generated or not AI, and YouTube runs its own detection too. AI involvement alone won't stop a track earning money. Separately, Deezer says a switch to hide AI-generated tracks, albums and artists arrives before the end of the year. In July it said about 90,000 tracks a day, more than half its uploads, were AI-made. Why it matters: If you use AI-generated music in ads, videos or in-store playlists, expect labelling and disclosure to become normal, and check the licence terms. Source: TechCrunch.
